I.

Rules and principles

[
1
]

These reasons relate to the defendants’
applications for dismissal of the plaintiff’s amended claims set out in Action
nos. S023786 and S023787, both in the Chilliwack Registry. For ease of
reference, I will refer to the first action as 786; the second as 787.

[
2
]

All the defendants have applied for an order
dismissing the plaintiff’s claims, relying, variously, on the following
Supreme
Court Civil Rules
: 1(3), 3(7)(9), 8-1, 8(2), 9-5(1), 9-6(4)-(5), and
21-8(1)(b).

A.

Rule 9-5

[
3
]

Under Rule 9-5(1) the court may strike a
pleading which:

a)         discloses no reasonable claim;

b)         is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or a vexatious;

c)         may prejudice, embarrassed or delay the fair hearing of
the proceeding, or is an abuse of process of the Court; and

d)         the court may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding
to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the application to be paid
as special costs.

[
4
]

Under Rule 9-5(1), It must be “plain and
obvious” the claim discloses no reasonable cause of action.”
Odhavji Estate
v. Woodhouse
,
2003 SCC 69
, para.
15
.

[
5
]

The court may give a party opportunity to
redraft an inadequate pleading. But if it is plain and obvious the redrafted
pleading is also bound to fail, the pleading should be struck:
Strata Plan
LMS3259 v. Sze Hang Holding Inc.
,
2009 BCSC 473
.

[
6
]

Pleadings may also be struck if:

a)         they are unintelligible, confusing and difficult to
understand;

b)         they do not establish a cause of action and do not
advance a claim known in law;

c)         they are without substance in that they are groundless,
fanciful and trifle with the court’s time; or

d)         they are not
bona fide
or oppressive and are
designed to cause the defendant’s anxiety, trouble and expense:
Dempsey v.
Envision Credit Union
,
2006 BCSC 750
, para.
17
;
Budgell v. Oppal
,

[2007] B.C.J. No. 1499 (S.C.), paras. 20-22
.

[
7
]

The pleadings must clearly define the issues of
fact and law for each of the issues the court must decide. The plaintiff must
plead facts essential to formulate a complete cause of action:
Canadian Bar
Assn. v. British Columbia
,
2008 BCCA 92
, paras.
59 – 60
;
Delaney
& Friends Cartoon Productions Ltd. v. Radical Entertainment Inc.
,
2005
BCSC 371
, para.
9
.

[
8
]

Material facts should be stated with certainty
and precision and in the natural order; and state the defendant’s wrongful acts
and the consequent damage:
Homalco Indian Band v. British Columbia
,
1998 CanLII 6658 (BC SC)
, [1998]
B.C.J. No. 2703 (S.C.).

[
9
]

When the plaintiff pleads several causes against
multiple defendants, they must clearly specify which facts relate to which
cause of action and to which defendant. If they fail to do so, they have not
clearly defined the issues of fact the court has to determine; thus making
their case subject to being struck by the court:
Stoneman v. Denman Island
Local Trust Committee
,
2010 BCSC 636
, para.
27
.

[
10
]

To determine whether it is plain and obvious the
statement of claim does not disclose a reasonable cause of action under Rule
9-5(1), facts are considered true; assumptions and speculations are not:
Dempsey
v. Envision Credit Union
,
2006 BCSC 750
, para.
7
;
McDaniel v.
McDaniel
,
2009 BCCA 53
[
McDaniel
], para.
22
;
Young v.
Borzoni,

2007 BCCA 16
, para.
30
.

[
11
]

For applications to strike pleadings under Rule
9-5(1) (b) and (c), on grounds they are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous,
vexatious, or may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial, if the
pleadings are so confusing it is difficult understand what is being claimed, the
applicant will have established relevancy and embarrassment. A pleading is
unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to establishment of the plaintiff’s
cause of action or does not advance any claim known to law.
Citizens for
Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160
(S.C.), para.
47
.

B.

Rule 9-6

[
12
]

Under Rule 9-6(4), an answering party who has
filed a defence on the party advancing claims against them may apply for
judgment dismissing all or part of a claim in the claiming party's originating
pleading. If satisfied the pleadings reveal no genuine issue for trial either
on a claim or defence, the court must pronounce judgment or dismiss the claim
accordingly:
Serup v. School District No. 57
,
[1989] B.C.J. No. 353
(C.A.)
.

[
13
]

The purpose of an application under Rule 9-6 is
to show the case already pleaded by the plaintiff is unsound or that the applicant
has a complete answer to it. In such circumstances, there is reason to weigh
the plaintiff’s pleadings in the scales against the defendants’ affidavit
evidence of the defendant:
McDaniel
, para.
18
.

[
14
]

Applications under Rule 9-6 require examination
of the pleaded facts to determine which causes of action they may support;
identification of the essential elements the plaintiff has to prove at trial to
succeed on each of the causes of action; and determination of whether the
plaintiff has pleaded sufficient material facts to support each element
required for each cause of action.
Skybridge Investments Ltd. v. Metro
Motors Ltd. (c.o.b. as Metro Ford)
,
2006 BCCA 500
[
Skybridge Investments
],
para.
10
. If the plaintiff has not pleaded sufficient material facts to
support each element of a cause of action, then “beyond a doubt that cause of
action is bound to fail and a defendant bringing an application pursuant to [Rule
9-6] will have met the onus to negative the existence of a
bona fide

triable issue.” (
Skybridge Investments
, para.
11
).

[
15
]

Further, if a defendant who applies under Rule
9-6 shows the case the plaintiff pleaded is unsound, or that they have a
complete answer to it, there is no logical reason to weigh the plaintiff’s
pleadings against the defendant’s affidavit evidence. In this case, the
plaintiff did not file a written response to the application or contradictory
affidavits.) Further, if the Court, without consideration of the plaintiff’s
pleadings, is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt they have no claim that
deserves to be tried, the defendant should succeed:
McDaniel
, para.
18
.

C.

Rule 4(2)

[
16
]

Rule 4(2) gives the court discretion to dismiss
an action if, in its opinion, the point of law substantially disposes of the
whole action or any distinct claim. The following principles govern the
exercise of that discretion:

(1)        the
point of law to be decided must be raised and clearly defined by the pleadings;

(2)        assuming
the opposite party's allegations are true, they must raise and support a claim
or defence in law;

(3)        the
facts relating to the point of law must not be in dispute and the point of law
must be capable of being resolved without hearing evidence;

(4)        the
determination of the question must be decisive of the litigation or a substantial
issue raised in it; and

(5)        the
court must be satisfied that there is some advantage in proceeding in this
manner in that it will greatly shorten the trial or result in a substantial
saving of costs.

[
Blanco-Arriba v.
British Columbia
,
[2001] B.C.J. No. 2376 (S.C.), para. 12
.]

[
17
]

A question of law can be decided even when it has
not been raised under Rule 9-4 (formerly Rule 34):
Nicholls v. Richmond
(Township)
,
[1983] B.C.J. No. 2298 (C.A.)
.

D.

Rule 21-8(1)(b)

[
18
]

Rule 21-8(1)(a), (b) and (c) provide:

(1)        A
party who has been served with an originating pleading or petition in a
proceeding, whether that service was effected in or outside British Columbia,
may, after filing a jurisdictional response in Form 108,

(a)        apply
to strike out the notice of civil claim, counterclaim, third party notice or petition
or to dismiss or stay the proceeding on the ground that the notice of civil
claim, counterclaim, third party notice or petition does not allege facts that,
if true, would establish that the court has jurisdiction over that party in
respect of the claim made against that party in the proceeding,

(b)        apply
to dismiss or stay the proceeding on the ground that the court does not have
jurisdiction over that party in respect of the claim made against that party in
the proceeding, or

(c)        allege in a
pleading or in a response to petition that the court does not have jurisdiction
over that party in respect of the claim made against that party in the
proceeding.

II.

Overview of
relationships and dealings between the plaintiff and the applicants

A.

Health Sciences Association
(“the HSA”)

[
19
]

The HSA is a trade union, certified to represent
health science professionals employed in the acute health and social services
health sectors. It is one of three constituent members of the Nurses Bargaining
Association (“NBA”) and the College of Registered Psychiatric Nurses of British
Columbia (the “College”). The College oversees the profession of registered
psychiatric nurses in the province, including their registration and disciplinary
matters.

[
20
]

At material times, the plaintiff was a member of
the HSA employed by Revera Long Term Care Inc. (“Revera”) as a registered
psychiatric nurse at its long-term health care facility, Holyrood Manor, where the
HSA was certified to represent the plaintiff and other psychiatric nurses
employed by Revera.

B.

Holyrood Manor and
Revera Long Term Care Inc. (“Revera”)

[
21
]

Revera operates Holyrood Manor, a private
long-term health care facility located in Maple Ridge, British Columbia. It
hired the plaintiff in March 2002. In September 2005, she secured a full-time
temporary position and, in September 2006, she became a full-time regular
employee. Revera terminated her employment for cause on March 6, 2009.

[
22
]

A collective agreement governed the terms and
conditions of the plaintiff’s employment, including termination. For its part,
Revera has characterized the essence of the plaintiff’s claim against it as a
labour relations dispute, over which the
British Columbia Labour Code
,
R.S.B.C. 196, c. 244

(“
L.R. Code”
) has exclusive
jurisdiction, and one outside the jurisdiction of the court.

C.

The College of
Registered Psychiatric Nurses (the “College”)

[
23
]

The plaintiff's claims against the College
relate to its role as statutory regulator of registered psychiatric nurses in
British Columbia. The plaintiff complaints are based primarily on how the
College received, investigated, and disposed of a complaint Revera lodged
against the plaintiff, who was at all material times a registered member of the
College. The College’s position, apart from that commonly held by all the other
applicants – which is that the plaintiff’s pleadings fail to comply with Master
McNaughton’s orders – is that the relief she seeks is not a matter for civil
liability; and, to the extent her claims can be made out at all, they are not
valid in law.

D.

Fraser Health Authority
(the “FHA”)

[
24
]

The Fraser Health Authority’s basic position is
that the plaintiff has failed to plead facts in support of her claims against
it of negligence, defamation;
Charter
infringements, abuse of process,
bad-faith bargaining, “dignitary tort”, violation of the of the
Freedom of
Information and Protection of Privacy Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 165 (the
“
FOIPPA
”), etc. on; and that the claims are not sound in law.

E.

Decker Management
(“Decker”)

[
25
]

Decker Management is an incorporated company
owned by a single shareholder. It engages in various business ventures,
including real estate development. It also owns and operates extended care
nursing care homes, which includes Simpson Manor (“Simpson”), a unionized facility
that had employed the plaintiff. Simpson is a licenced hospital and unionized
facility. It provides extended care beds paid partly by the Fraser Health
Authority.

[
26
]

The plaintiff worked for Decker as a psychiatric
nurse on a casual basis between May 26, 2005 and October 13, 2007, the date of
her last shift. She was removed from the call-in list on September 12, 2008.
She was a member of the British Columbia Nurses Union, which represented her.

[
27
]

Decker submits the plaintiff’s claims are
irreparably flawed. In essence, they relate, in some way, to how Dexter
terminated her employment. Dexter says, the claims are irreparably flawed,
inter
alia
, because they lie outside the jurisdiction of this court and the scope
of the
FOIPPA
which does not apply to Decker in the circumstances of
this case.

III.

History of proceedings

[
28
]

The following history of proceedings is relevant
to relief sought by all the applicants.

[
29
]

December 16, 2009, the plaintiff filed two
Notices of Civil Claim for Action Nos. S23786 (“786”) and S23787 (“787”).
The facts and allegations against the defendants in each action are similar.

[
30
]

December 10, 2012, Master MacNaughton conducted
a Case Planning Conference. She ordered the plaintiff to amend each of her
Notices of Civil Claim (“NCCs”) before January 11, 2013, to:

a)         correctly
name all the existing defendants;

b)         identify
and specify the relief claimed as against each named defendant; and,

c)         specify the
legal basis for the relief sought against each named defendant.

[
31
]

The plaintiff then filed three subsequent amended
NCCs in each action, on January 11, January 14, and January 23, 2013,
respectively. None of these amended NCCs complied with Master McNaughton’s Case
Plan Orders.

[
32
]

On February 14, 2013, Master MacNaughton
conducted a second Case Planning Conference, this time, focused on inadequacies
in the amended NCCs. She ordered the amended NCCs be struck from the Court
Registry and ordered the plaintiff to file amended NCCs for each action, on or
before February 24, 2013, in compliance with the Original Order, as detailed
above. Among the other orders made were these:

a)         correctly
name all the existing defendants;

b)         identify
and specify the relief claimed as against each named defendant; and,

c)         specify the
legal basis for the relief sought against each named defendant.

[
33
]

On March 8, 2013, the plaintiff filed her amended
NCCs for each action.

A.

Findings on the flaws
in the plaintiff’s pleadings

[
34
]

All the applicants agree with the HSA’s
submissions that the plaintiff failed to clarify her pleadings against them in
a manner that complied with Master McNaughton’s orders. I agree those with
those assertions.

[
35
]

All the applicants submit the plaintiff’s claims
remain confusing and deeply flawed, amended versions little better than the
previous, sometimes worse; leaving the applicants, even after many hours of
painstaking review, trying to trace a logical line in and through the claims; afterwards
still remaining doubtful about which specific claim might apply to which party,
what relief the plaintiff sought; and against which defendant. Perusal of the
pleadings reveals the difficulties. To figure out what it is the plaintiff
claims as against them, and the relief she seeks, generous and sweeping
assumptions have to be fully deployed without assurances the guesswork is
correct.

[
36
]

In some cases, a plaintiff’s self-representation
may call for a liberal reading of their pleadings; but not for the level of
guesswork the defendants have had to engage in to gain a sense of what it is
the plaintiff claims against them. The plaintiff does not lack education or
intelligence; she should be able to state simply the basic facts required to
state an actionable case. I found, however, she lacked not the ability to state
the necessary facts for an action; rather, none of the facts she could assemble
could support any action. What the plaintiff has done, effectively, is
nominalise a series of unspecified possible actions against the defendants into
a possible cause of action; for example: ‘the defendants may have been guilty
of negligence; the defendants may be guilty of defamation; the defendants may
have been guilty of [a]
Charter
breach’, and so on. Based only on the
pleadings’ failure to conform either to the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
(“the

Rules
”) or to Master McNaughton’s order, the defendants are entitled to
succeed and to see all the plaintiff’s claims against them dismissed.

[
37
]

Not only had the Master extended herself to
assist the plaintiff. An arbitration and Labour Relations Board (“LRB”) addressed
the substance of the same complaints she evokes against the defendants. Throughout,
the plaintiff had counsel, retained by the HSA, although not legally obliged to
do so. A comprehensive arbitrated settlement was reached, with the plaintiff
having the benefit of legal counsel’s advice.

[
38
]

Based on the foregoing, all the plaintiff’s claims
ought to be dismissed and summary judgment entered in all the defendants’
favour. However, as the order is final, I have considered, and will address,
the nature of the plaintiff’s putative claims and the applicants’ various
extensive and scrupulous responses to them. Common to all the defendants’
applications is the submission that the plaintiff has failed to adhere to the
orders Master McNaughton made. There are also elements of redundancy in some
aspects of the defendant’s submissions – for example, on the point of this Court’s
lack of jurisdiction to hear the case. I have attempted to avoid redundancy;
where it is necessary to focus on aspects more specific to an applicant’s
situation. The materials were voluminous; I will not mention all the points
raised by the applicants and the plaintiff, which I have considered.

[
39
]

The defendants provided written outlines of
their oral submissions, amply supported by documents and affidavits which
summarize the nature and extent of the defendant’s relevant dealings with the
plaintiff. Their submissions and their supporting materials comply with the
Rules

and the governing principles I reviewed earlier at the start of these reasons.

[
40
]

At the conclusion of the hearing, pending
reasons, I made an order to prohibit the plaintiff from taking any further
steps in the litigation, enjoined against her commencing any new actions, and,
as she intended to join additional parties also enjoined against her adding any
other parties.

[
41
]

Based on the materials, the governing principles
and authorities, all the defendants have succeeded.

[
42
]

I turn now to the nature of the plaintiff’s
claims, and the reasons additional to the plaintiff’s failure to comply with
Master McNaughton’s orders and to the
Rules
, why the defendants must
succeed.

IV.

Application of the health sciences
association

A.

General nature of
complaints

[
43
]

The HSA characterizes the essence of the
plaintiff’s claims as ones that allege it failed to represent the plaintiff
adequately on the following matters: termination of her employment by
Revera/Holyrood Manor; suspension of her professional licence by the College of
Registered Psychiatric Nurses of British Columbia (the “College”); and in its
failure to secure a certain benefit said the plaintiff claims was owed her as a
“displaced nurse”. This last item refers to a settlement agreement reached between
nursing unions and the provincial government. It entitled some nurses to financial
compensation following a Supreme Court of Canada ruling against the provincial
government.

[
44
]

On a preliminary point of pleadings, the HSA
points out the plaintiff does not allege in her further amended NCC 787 that
the HSA represented her in her dealings with Simpson Hospital (another
defendant, whose application will be considered further on in these reasons).
In fact, the HSA was not certified to represent registered psychiatric nurses
at the Simpson facility or other facilities operated by the defendant, Decker
Management Ltd., and the HSA never represented her when she worked at its
Simpson Manor facility. Further, although the plaintiff named Ridge Meadows
Hospital &/or Fraser Health Authority as defendants in her further amended
NCC, she does not allege that the HSA represented her at Maple Ridge Meadows
Hospital; and admits that neither Maple Ridge Meadows Hospital nor Fraser
Health employed her.

B.

Plaintiff’s Collective
Agreement grievance as it relates to Holyrood Manor/Revera termination

[
45
]

The plaintiff filed three Collective Agreement
grievances while she worked employed at Holyrood Manor. The last of these
related to Holyrood’s March 6, 2009 termination of her employment. About a week
earlier, Holyrood filed its own formal complaint with the College, related to
the alleged professional misconduct that had led to termination of her
employment. On May 4, 2009, the College suspended her licence.

[
46
]

The HSA had no contractual obligation to become
involved in matters related to professional discipline, which is the College’s
responsibility. But because the professional complaint to the College and the
plaintiff’s termination by Revera intersected somewhat, the HSA, following an
internal informal discretionary practice, elected to retain counsel to assist
the plaintiff at the College’s hearing and at a subsequent LRB review.

[
47
]

In July 2009, the plaintiff met with a
representative of the HSA and her legal counsel to discuss a settlement
agreement that contained certain conditions that would allow her to regain her
licence to practice as a psychiatric nurse and become reinstated as a member of
the College. On July 16, 2009, the plaintiff; her counsel, retained on her
behalf by the HSA; representatives of the HSA; and Revera, the employer,
attended a mediation/arbitration hearing on the plaintiff’s Termination
Grievance. Before the Arbitrator, they reached a settlement, signed and
witnessed by the plaintiff, Holyrood Manor, the HSA, and Revera. It confirmed,
among other things, that the plaintiff withdrew her Termination Grievance; the
employer withdrew its termination notice; the plaintiff resigned her
employment, effective July 16, 2009; would receive a lump sum payment of
$20,000, less statutory deductions; and that the employer would provide her a
neutral letter of reference. The settlement included a mutual release stating:

The parties
hereby release one another from any and all liability with respect to any and
all actions, claims, etc. which have arisen or may arise regarding the
Grievor’s employment with the Employer, including all claims arising under the
Employment Standards Act or the Human Rights Code. The Grievor releases both
the Employer and the Union [HSA] from any and all liability in this regard.

[
48
]

The settlement was carried out. The plaintiff
ceased being a member of the HSA and, since then, she has not worked at a
workplace where the HSA has certification rights.

1.

Significance of the
plaintiff’s grievance before the LRB

[
49
]

Despite the plaintiff’s having signed a
settlement agreement that paid her a $22,000 settlement, in September 2009, she
went on to file a grievance against the HSA with the LRB. Her complaints fell
under the general rubric of the HSA’s duty to provide its members fair
representation, as required of it by s. 12(1) of the
L.R. Code
. Her
complaint consisted of two main parts: 1) The HSA’s allegedly inadequate
representation of her regarding the College’s suspension of her professional
licence and regarding her Collective Agreement grievance against Revera; and 2)
to the HSA’s alleged failure to represent her interests adequately with respect
to the Bill 29 settlement. (As mentioned earlier, a settlement reached by the
government and nursing labour unions allowed any nurse affected by parts of
Bill 29 to seek compensation.) The plaintiff claimed her circumstances matched
the definition of a displaced nurse under the settlement; and, in April 2009,
she began asking for compensation. The HSA took the position the plaintiff’s
circumstances did not match the definition of a displaced nurse and that she
was not eligible anyway because she failed to apply within the required time
required.

[
50
]

The LRB dismissed all the plaintiff’s complaints
on their merits, because her complaints were encompassed within her employment

C.

Legal points and
conclusions

1.

College’s statutory
protections

[
97
]

Before briefly disposing of the plaintiff’s
individual claims, I should first note that the
DAPA
and the
HPA
,
give the College statutory immunity from the plaintiff’s claims, leaving no
genuine issue to be tried.

[
98
]

Section 1
of the
DAPA
provides:

1 If,

(a) by an Act a
corporation is established having as one of its purposes the regulation of the
profession or occupation practised or carried on by the members of the
corporation, and

(b) disciplinary
powers over the members of the corporation in respect of their conduct in the
profession or occupation regulated are conferred by the Act on the corporation,
or on any body of its members, or on any official or member of the corporation,

no liability is
incurred by the corporation, or by any body of the members, or by any official
or member of the corporation, or by any person retained as counsel, solicitor
or agent by the corporation for any act or thing done in the exercise of the
disciplinary powers conferred or in doing any act or thing in preparation for
the exercise of those powers, unless the act or thing is done maliciously and
without reasonable and probable cause.

[
99
]

Section 15 of the
HPA
and Nurses
(Registered Psychiatric)
B.C. Regulation 285/2008
establish the College as a
disciplinary corporation empowered to deal with disciplinary matters for
registered psychiatric nurses. The plaintiff’s claims relate directly to disciplinary
matters and they engage the College’s disciplinary powers:
Netupsky v.
Association of Professional Engineers & Geoscientists of British Columbia
,

[2001] B.C.J. No. 1443 (S.C.), paras. 5
, 7, and 11.

[
100
]

The College does not have statutory immunity when it acts in a
malicious way, or without reasonable and probable cause, but the plaintiff has
not alleged this, leaving no genuine issue for trial:
Allen v. College of
Dental Surgeons of British Columbia
,
[2005] B.C.J. No. 1285 (S.C.), paras. 31-32
.

[
101
]

Section 24
of the
HPA
extends immunity
for actions or omissions in good faith:

Immunity for acts or omissions in good faith

24(1) No action for damages lies or may be
brought against a member of a board or a person acting on behalf of or under
the direction of a board or college because of anything done or omitted in good
faith

(a) in the
performance or intended performance of any duty under this Act, or

(b) in the
exercise or intended exercise of any power under this Act.

(2) Subsection
(1) does not absolve a college from vicarious liability for an act or omission
for which it would be vicariously liable if this section were not in force.

[
102
]

The plaintiff has not pleaded any facts, per
s. 24(2)
of the
Charter
,
to support a claim it acted vicariously for any other party. Absent bad faith,
which is not pleaded, anything the College had done or has failed to do when it
carried out its powers of investigation and discipline is not actionable, and
her claims against the College must be dismissed on those grounds alone.

[
103
]

As for the plaintiff’s claims regarding the hearing process, these
devolve to questions of procedural fairness or breaches of natural justice,
which do not constitute a valid civil action. Remedies for such complaints fall
within the realm of Administrative Law:
Monogram Properties Ltd. v.
Etobicoke

(1996), 34 M.P.L.R. (2d) 48 (Ont. Gen. Div.), para. 18
,
cited in
Roeder v. Lang Michener Lawrence & Shaw
,
2007 BCCA 152
, paras.
19-20
.
The plaintiff has not claimed that the College failed to comply with the
requirements of its enabling statute.

[
104
]

To the extent a most liberal reading makes possible, a claim for
abuse of process, or one tainted by negligent action and omissions, the
plaintiff does not state facts to establish the College proceeded with
collateral or improper purpose, engaged in an act or made any threat, overt or
otherwise, to further illegitimate purposes.

[
105
]

The plaintiff did not plead any facts that would establish any of
the essential elements of an action in negligence. I discussed earlier the
plaintiff’s claims related to the
FOIPPA
when I discussed the
application of the HSA. They have no application or merit here either. And, for
much the same reasons as discussed earlier in the HSA’s application, none of the
plaintiff’s
Charter
claims against the College have any merit. Further,
the plaintiff has not pleaded facts against the College that would establish
any basis for a
Charter
claim against it. Neither has she established
any basis in her pleadings for either the presence of a fiduciary duty or a
breach of it.

[
106
]

In summary, I find the plaintiff’s claims, either individually or
combined, do not disclose material facts to support any action against the
College. Neither do they raise a genuine triable issue for trial. Further, the
HPA

and the
DAPA
provide the College a complete defence.

VI.

Application of decker management ltd. &
simpson hospital application

A.

Overview

[
107
]

Decker Management Ltd. is a company, owned by a soul shareholder,
(“Decker”). It operates Simpson Hospital, before July 2008 known as Simpson

Hospital
Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 200 [
HA
].

[
108
]

The plaintiff worked for Decker as a registered psychiatric nurse,
starting in 2005 on a casual basis; ending with her last shift on October 13,

earlier, Simpson Manor was unionized. A collective agreement negotiated by the

[
109
]

that an inspector been appointed to investigate the professional conduct and

“subject to the conditions outlined in the
FOIPPA
.” Decker understood
this to mean the College would treat disclosed information confidentially and,
according to an affidavit sworn by Mr. I. Riesen, the chief financial and
operating officer of Decker, its disclosure to the College would not constitute
a breach of the
FOIPPA
. The College’s inspector questioned Mr. Riesen
and other Decker representatives about the plaintiff’s attendance on shifts.
Decker says its sole motive in providing the requested information was to
permit the College to discharge its supervisory and disciplinary obligations.
The College’s investigation was actually first initiated by a complaint filed by
Holyrood Manor, another former employer of the plaintiff. As mentioned, the
plaintiff’s and Holyrood’s grievances and the College’s inquiry devolved into a
consent agreement of undertaking.

[
110
]

Decker aptly distills the plaintiff’s
allegations against it in para. 17 of its outline of submissions:

17.       … Decker’s
participation in the investigation was wrongful and that its communication
regarding her work history with the Inspector amounted, inter alia, to a breach
of
FoIPPA
, negligence, and defamation. Ms. McGregor also makes a
number of other allegations that Decker failed to discharge its obligations to
her under the Collective Agreement, including in connection with its
termination of her employment.

[
111
]

Decker submits all the claims related to the investigation should be
dismissed or struck out on grounds any disclosure Decker made to the College
during its investigation were made on an occasion of absolute privilege, or
were otherwise protected by witness immunity. All other claims should be
dismissed or struck because they fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of LRB
and are outside the jurisdiction of this court.

[
112
]

I agree with Decker that the combination of its immunity and its
jurisdictional argument are sufficient to dispose of the plaintiff’s claims.

B.

Jurisdictional
arguments

[
113
]

Decker relies on Rule 9-5 for striking the pleadings and Rule 21-8
for its position on jurisdiction. Decker filed its jurisdictional response
September 4, 2012, after it had filed its response to the plaintiff’s civil
claim. Decker’s jurisdiction defence is based on the subject matter of the
dispute, not its territory. This is not a situation that may occur when a
defendant asserts the court lacks territorial jurisdiction, but is found to
have effectively attorned to it, depending on when it raises the jurisdictional
point of law and other considerations. Decker does not dispute the territorial
jurisdiction, as the plaintiff appears to have thought: territorial
jurisdiction is not an issue, subject matter jurisdiction is. Further, even if
Decker wanted to attorn to the Court’s subject matter jurisdiction, it could
not do so because such action would represent an attempt to frustrate the Legislature’s
intention to remove jurisdiction of the subject matter from the court,
Rothgiesser
v. Rothgiesser
,
2000 CanLII 1153 (ON CA)
, [2000] O.J. No. 33 (Ont. C.A.).

[
114
]

It is appropriate for Decker to seek relief under Rule 9-5, as the
plaintiff’s claim falls outside the jurisdiction of the court; rendering the
claim unreasonable within the meaning of Rule 9-5 (1)(a) or embarrassing, per
(1)(c):
Sykes v. Langara College
,
[1997] B.C.J. No. 1295 (S.C.)
;
and
Musqueam Indian Band v. British Columbia
,
[1991] B.C.J. No. 2288
(S.C.)
, para.4.

[
115
]

I have already discussed the exclusive jurisdiction of LRB under the

L.R.

Code
on collective agreements and other labour relations
matters. But I will briefly canvas aspects of it here again, and include additional
points amplified by Decker. What is stated here, applies there, and vice-versa.

[
116
]

The Collective Agreement that governed the plaintiff’s employment
contained an arbitration provision; s. 84(2) of the
L.R.

Code

requires it; stating that [a collective agreement] “must contain a provision
governing dismissal or discipline of an employee bound by the agreement”. The
collective agreement gave either party the right to “refer any grievance,
dispute or difference [unresolved through a grievance procedure] to a Board of
Arbitration or a single arbitrator. Article 10.01 (B)-(C) of the Nurses’
Collective Agreement states that any decision of the arbitrator “shall be final
and binding upon the parties”.

[
117
]

The Supreme Court of Canada rejected
jurisdiction models that would have labour arbitrators and Superior Courts
share jurisdiction. It adopted an “exclusive jurisdiction” model. In
Weber
,
referred to in the HSA’s application, the court said at paras. 43 and 52:

[43]      … The issue is not whether the
action, defined legally, is independent of the collective agreement, but rather
whether the dispute is one “arising under [the] collective agreement”. Where
the dispute, regardless of how it may be characterized legally, arises under
the collective agreement, then the jurisdiction to resolve it lies exclusively
with the labor tribunal and the courts cannot try it.

…

[52]      … The
question in each case is whether the dispute, in its essential character,
arises from the interpretation, application, administration or violation of the
collective agreement.

[
118
]

At para. 53, the court explained that an express provision
dealing precisely with the dispute is not necessary and that the matter can
arise under a collective agreement inferentially or by implication.

[
119
]

Decker takes the position, as did the HSA, both correctly, that the
plaintiff’s complaints against Decker relate to matters governed by the
Collective Agreement and the exclusive jurisdiction of the LRB. The plaintiff
effectively acknowledges the LRB’s jurisdiction at para. 2 of her further
amended claim, where she states that “Simpson Hospital may also be liable for
breach of the terms of employment called the collective agreement”. The
plaintiff alleges, in effect, wrongful dismissal and other matters, all related
to the manner in which Decker terminated her employment, which is governed by
Article 15.04 and article 3 of the Collective Agreement; as an inclusion required
by s. 84 of the
L.R. Code
. Further, as counsel for Decker points
out, at para. 53 of
Weber
, the court specifically identified
allegations of “wrongful dismissal” and “constructive dismissal” as claims
within the exclusive jurisdiction of the labour arbitrator.

[
120
]

Counsel noted that the plaintiff’s amended claim
has some of the Article numbers of the Collective Agreement struck through. She
also slightly changed the wording of her claims from “employment contract,
called the collective agreement,” to “terms of employment called the collective
agreement” These changes do not change the essential nature of the plaintiff’s
claims as ones arising from or under the Collective Agreement that governed her
employment at all material times, as counsel stated it. Counsel also rightly
noted that the same disputed matters that allegedly constitute breaches of the
Collective Agreement form the basis for other causes of action: positing names
of other causes of action does not transform the subject matter from one inside
to one outside the jurisdiction of the LRB. Counsel stated the point well this
way:

As set out in
Weber
,
the plaintiff’s attempts to obfuscate the nature of her Claim by striking
through her references to the various Collective Agreement articles, or to
claim the breaches of the Collective Agreement may also constitute other claims
in tort or under statute does not somehow give the Court jurisdiction. It does
not matter how claim is framed legally. If its substance or underlying factual
matrix is a dispute arising under collective agreement, the agreement cannot be
heard in this court.

C.

Decker’s immunity
defence

[
121
]

The general rule is clear that no action lies for defamatory
statements contained in a document properly used in the course of proceedings
before any court of justice or tribunal the law recognizes. The rule applies to
tribunals exercising functions equivalent to courts of justice:
Sussman v.
Eales

(1985), 33 C.C.L.T. 156 (Ont. H.C.J.), pp. 157-8
, appeal allowed
in part
(1986) 25 C.P.C. (2d) 7 (Ont. C.A.)
, as cited in
Hung v. Gardiner
,

2003 BCCA 257
, para.
6
.

[
122
]

The immunity will only be conferred upon a citizen complaining in a
confidential way to a body created by statute. The court in
Sussman

noted that a communication of that kind can hardly be said to be a publication
of the kind that is apt to harm one's reputation in the community to a degree
sufficient to attract an award of compensation,
Sussman
, pp. 159-60;

Hung
, para.
7
.

[
123
]

The doctrine applies to statements made to a disciplinary body,
Hung
,
para.
8
, citing
Lincoln v. Daniels
,
[1961] 3 All E.R.740, p. 748
.
The immunity applies to any claim made on communications with the professional
body, irrespective of how the plaintiff frames their claim:
Hung
, para.
34
.

[
124
]

As discussed in the College’s application, the
HPA
is the
College’s governing legislation, empowering and obliging it to investigate
complaints made against a registrant: s. 32(2), 33(1). The Inquiry Committee
and the inquiry process set out in the
HPA
constitute legislated stages
of the College’s disciplinary processes. The inspector appointed by the Inquiry
Committee and their subsequent inspection is also an integral part of the disciplinary
process, initiated at the College’s discretion. It may lead, at the College’s
discretion and at its direction, to a settlement, as occurred here, or to the
issue of a citation against the registrant and further disciplinary proceedings
and hearings. The fact the College exercised its discretion through a
settlement and stipulations the plaintiff was required to follow if she wished
her licence to be reinstated does not in any way diminish the fact that the
College at all material times was acting in its capacity as a professional
disciplinary body, or render actionable communications between itself, Decker
and others, from whom the inspector or other duly authorized person solicited
and received information deemed relevant to the complaint and its investigation
by the College.

[
125
]

Decker is immune from any claim, howsoever constituted, related in
any way to information it provided to the College at its request.

[
126
]

As for claims related to the
FOIPPA
, I have disposed of that,
generally, earlier. I agree with counsel for Decker that the plaintiff has not
pleaded anything to show that it did anything more than comply with directions
it received from the College in its Investigation Notice; and that its
communications with the Inspector fully complied with the
FOIPPA
and the

Personal Information Protection Act
, S.B.C. 2003, c. 63 [
PIPA
].
The
PIPA
applies to Decker a private for profit extended care private
hospital licenced under Part 2 of the
HA
and does not meet the
definitions of hospital set out in
s. 1
of the
HA
.

[
127
]

Further, as set out in Mr. Riesen’s affidavit, while Decker’s
agreement with the FHA is subject to the requirements of the
FOIPPA
, the
agreement also provides it does not apply to the Decker’s information,
documents, or records that relate solely to its internal labour and employment
matters.

[
128
]

Authorization similar to
s. 33.1(1)
(c) and
(1) of the

FOIPPA
, which authorizes disclosures to disciplinary bodies, is
found at
s. 18(1)
of the
PIPA
, which authorizes disclosure of
personal information without the consent of the individual if:

(i)         the
disclosure is for the purpose of complying with a subpoena, warrant or order
issued or made by a court, person or body with jurisdiction to compel the
production of personal information,

…

(o)        the
disclosure is required or authorized by law.

[
129
]

Accordingly, both the
FOIPPA
and
PIPA
except
disclosures authorized by law. Further, and as set out in
s. 28
of the
HPA
,
and as recited by the College in the Inspection Notice it sent to Decker, an
inspector may, subject to limitations imposed on them by the Inquiry Committee,
and without court order, “investigate, inquire into, inspect, observe or
examine” records of the registrant related to their practice of her profession
[as a psychiatric nurse].

[
130
]

In short, the inspector was authorized to compel production of the
information it sought from Decker; and no matter which privacy legislation
Decker fell under, whether
ss. 33(1)
(c) and
33.1(1)
of
FOIPPA
or

s. 18(1)
(o) of
PIPA
; Decker was protected, disclosure of its
employment information in its possession being for the purpose of the College’s
investigating of the plaintiff, a person whose professional practice it
regulated, and in which capacity it had the right to obtain employment
information from Decker, and Decker the obligation to provide.

D.

Defamation,
Charter
and
other claims

[
131
]

I agree the plaintiff has not raised a genuine issue to be tried on
the plaintiff’s defamation claim. In addition, however, Decker also relies on a
limitation defence. As noted elsewhere, briefly here again, the plaintiff is
out of time on any claim for defamation, her NCCs having been filed more than
two years after the alleged defamations; and also before June 1, 2013, hence
governed by the 1996
Limitation Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, not the
2013 version; see
Limitation Act
, S.B.C. 2012, c. 13, s. 30(3).

[
132
]

The facts do not support any postponement of
time. Section 6(3) does not include defamation actions as one that may benefit
from a postponement of the running of time. In any case, the discoverability
principle is concerned with the discovery of facts, not with “learning about
the laws of tort or defamation”. Section 6(4) provides:

(4) Time does not begin to run against a
plaintiff with respect to an action referred to in subsection (3) until the
identity of the defendant is known to the plaintiff and those facts within the
plaintiff's means of knowledge are such that a reasonable person, knowing those
facts and having taken the appropriate advice a reasonable person would seek on
those facts, would regard those facts as showing that

(a) an action on
the cause of action would, apart from the effect of the expiration of a
limitation period, have a reasonable prospect of success, and

(b) the person whose means of knowledge is
in question ought, in the person's own interests and taking the person's
circumstances into account, to be able to bring an action.

[
133
]

Further, the plaintiff has no prospect of success. As counsel points
out, the plaintiff ‘discovered’ tort and other remedies on September 16, 2009,
which is when she filed her complaints under s. 12 of the
L.R. Code

and before the expiry of two years.

[
134
]

As for the plaintiff’s
Charter
related claims, as discussed
on the application of HSA, the plaintiff has not raised any genuine
Charter

breaches to be tried. Furthermore, the
Charter
does not apply to Decker:
it does not perform government activities, such as carrying out a government
program; it is as a private for profit company operating independently of
government. See:
Eldridge v. British Columbia (Attorney General)
,
1997 CanLII 327 (SCC)
, [1997]
3 S.C.R. 624, paras.
44 and 53
. See also:
Stoffman v. Vancouver General
Hospital
,
1990 CanLII 62 (SCC)
, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 483. I agree with Decker that its activities were
not sufficiently, governmental, if at all; and, more important, within the
jurisdiction of the LRB.

[
135
]

In summary: the plaintiff’s claims fall within the jurisdiction of
the LRB and this Court has no jurisdiction over them. Communications between
Decker and the College are protected by absolute immunity.
FOIPPA
does
not apply to Decker and the occasion, purposes, and legal setting in which the
information transmitted by Decker were legal, and it is fully protected from
the plaintiff’s claims. The plaintiff’s defamation claims are out of time;
there are no genuine
Charter
issues to be tried; the nature of Decker’s
operations and the relationship between the plaintiff and Decker fall outside
the ambit of the
Charter
. Further, the plaintiff’s claims do not comply
with the
Rules
or with the orders of Master McNaughton. There is no
genuine issue to try.

[
136
]

The plaintiff’s claims against Decker are struck and her case
dismissed.

Holyrood manor and revera long term care

[
137

139

140

[
141
]

The senior labor relations officer for the union wrote Revera on March
12, 2009, giving notice it intended to grieve the plaintiff’s termination and

[
142
]

The Memorandum of Agreement was signed by the plaintiff and a
representative of Revera, on the following terms, mentioned earlier, set out

a)         the Union will withdraw its grievance;

b)         the plaintiff will resign her employment, effective July
16, 2009;

c)         Revera will pay the plaintiff $20,000, less statutory

d)         Revera will provide the plaintiff with a neutral
reference letter; and

[
143
]

As discussed in earlier sections of these Reasons, such as the section
dealing with the HSA’s application, after the plaintiff settled, she proceeded
to file a complaint under s. 12 of the
L.R. Code
on the HSA’s
handling of her dismissal grievance, s. 12 prohibiting, as it does,
arbitrary, discriminatory or bad faith actions by the union in their
representation of an employee.

[
144
]

After the LRB dismissed the complaint, the plaintiff applied for
leave and reconsideration, which the LRB denied on December 16, 2009, finding

during her employment by:

a)         wrongfully dismissing her contrary to the terms of
employment;

b)         suspending her without notice in breach of the terms of
her employment;

c)         conducting biased investigation processes in breach of
the terms of employment;

d)         failing to refer a perceived problem for internal
assessment;

e)         failing to comply with an order the arbitrator;

f)          failing to provide yearly work evaluations, a term of
employment;

g)         failing to remove past records of suspension, the term of
employment;

h)        failing to remove the letter as ordered by the arbitrator;

i)          making inappropriate deductions to the plaintiff’s
paycheck and settlement check;

j)          failing to provide a proper payment to the plaintiff;

k)         failing to provide proper severance;

l)          displacing the plaintiff in breach of the terms of
employment;

m)        providing confidential information and laying a complaint
with the College;

n)        providing confidential information the College and Service
Canada about the plaintiff without authorization and in breach of the terms of employment;
and

o)         providing inaccurate information to the College and EI
programs.

[
145
]

In its February 8, 2013 response, Revera filed a response and
denied,
inter alia
, the court’s jurisdiction.

A.

Rule 21-8

[
146
]

Rule 21-8(b) allows the court to dismiss or stay a proceeding on
grounds it does not have jurisdiction.

[
147
]

I have twice already discussed
Weber v. Ontario Hydro
,
1995 CanLII 108 (SCC)
, [1995]
2 S.C.R. 929 [
Weber
] and
Webber v. Kelowna (City)

2001 BCSC 189
,
and will not go over the principles those cases stand for here, except to
briefly note again that in
Weber
, the Supreme Court held the plaintiff’s
tort action and
Charter
claim could not stand, as it was precluded by
the terms of a Collective Agreement and the Ontario equivalent of the
L.R.
Code
. The plaintiff’s complaints against Revera are clearly governed by the
Collective Agreement and fall within the jurisdiction of the LRB.

[
148
]

Counsel for Revera points out the court may grant leave for a point
of law to be determined on summary hearing and then go on to determine that
point of law upon finding it is in the interests of a just speedy and
inexpensive determination and that the question can be decided on assumed facts
that arise from the pleadings.
Nicholls v. Richmond (Township)
(1983),

1983 CanLII 431 (BC CA)
, 43 B.C.L.R. 162, para.
7
.

[
149
]

Revera, Decker and the HSA meet the threshold test for summary
disposition set out in
Blanco-Arriba v. British Columbia
,
2001 BCSC
1557
, paras.
20-31
. The pleadings identify the facts that identifies the
relevant point of law; the point of law asserted is that the plaintiff’s
employment with Revera was subject to the Collective Agreement; Revera HSA
pleaded it and relies on it; and, even if the plaintiff’s claims were true,
those facts cannot support a claim if the court has no jurisdiction over them.
Further, the point of law can be resolved without hearing evidence, as the
existence of the Collective Agreement, standing alone, determines jurisdiction;
and the court’s answer to that question decides the litigation: if in the
applicant’s favour, the court must dismiss the plaintiff’s claim. Finally,
proceeding summarily will result in substantial cost savings.

B.

Effects of the binding
settlement agreement between the parties

[
150
]

I agree with Revera that a binding settlement agreement was reached
between the parties on all matters relating to the plaintiff’s employment with
Revera. It encompassed not only matters transpired before the settlement, but
also future claims. The plaintiff has not stated any facts to support the
suggestion in her further amended NCC claims that the settlement agreement may
be “illegal”, a question which, anyway, is a matter for the arbitrator to
determine. The LRB did so, in effect, after the plaintiff filed her complaint
with it. The LRB determined the plaintiff signified her agreement with the
settlement by signing it and that she was properly represented by counsel.

[
151
]

The plaintiff has never returned the $20,000 settlement she
received.

[
152
]

I agree with counsel’s submission that the plaintiff’s claims
against Revera are encompassed within the settlement agreement and settled by
it, the LRB tribunal confirmed this, it has become
res judicata
, and
this court has no jurisdiction, which constitutes them an abuse of process
under Rule 9-5(1)(d); and on that basis alone should be struck.

C.

Limitation Act
and
breach of
Charter
claims

[
153
]

Revera also relies on the
Limitation Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, s. 3(2); submitting that the two-year
limitation period applies. Subsections (2) and (a) state:

(2)        After the expiration of 2 years
after the date on which the right to do so arose a person may not bring any of
the following actions:

(a)        subject to
subsection (4)(k), for damages in respect of injury to person or property,
including economic loss arising from the injury, whether based on contract,
tort or statutory duty.

[
154
]

This would encompass all of what the plaintiff has set out in Part 2
of her Amended Notice of Civil Claim, “all negligent actions and omission, all
torts of the defendants that caused harm to the plaintiff, including, but not
limited to, economic interference, dignity tort”,
Bush v. Vancouver (City)
,

2006 BCSC 1207
, para.
36
;
Foote v. Canada (Attorney General)
,
2012
BCSC 177
, paras.
29 and 30
.

[
155
]

With respect to the plaintiff’s
Charter
claims, these can be
disposed of by their lack of factual correspondence with the intentions of the
various sections the plaintiff asserts; further, by the court’s lack of
jurisdiction, the Release the plaintiff signed includes all claims, and Holyrood’s
limitation defence.

[
156
]

Further, for the reasons already given in the section dealing with
Decker’s application, the
Charter
does not apply to Revera.

[
157
]

The plaintiff’s claim against Revera is dismissed.

VIII.

Application of Fraser
Health authority and meadow ridge hospital

[
158
]

The FHA provides a wide variety of health services on both sides of
the Fraser River. They include hospitals, health clinics, residential care,
assisted living homes, and community health care centres. It seeks dismissal of
the plaintiff’s amended NCC, (Action 787) under Rule 9-5(1) because it fails to
disclose a reasonable cause of action against it, and under Rule 9-6 because
they reveal no genuine issue for trial.

[
159
]

I will not repeat the FHA’s complaints regarding the shortcomings in
the plaintiff’s pleadings as they cover the same ground as do the other
parties’ submissions, and with the same accepted justification.

[
160
]

Similarly with the College and the other defendants, the plaintiff’s
claims against the FHA relate primarily to their alleged involvement in the
events that led to the plaintiff’s dismissal from her employment at Holyrood
Manor in 2009.

[
161
]

At para 14, Part 2 of her further amended NCC
787, the plaintiff claims:

The defendant
hospital representatives made several misleading and negligent statements
pertaining to the Plaintiff which may be defamation, discrimination, innuendo,
altered, and misleading, meant to cause harm to the Plaintiff. [Underline emphasis
removed.]

[
162
]

The plaintiff summarizes her claims against the
defendants, including the FHA, in paras. 3 to 11 of NCC 787. I have
referred to some of these earlier, and will not recite all of them here, but
will select types representative of them:

3.         The
following torts…: duty to minimize, duty of standard, duty of care, breaches to
the terms of employment, common law, including equity, duty to provide warning,
due diligence, arbitrary treatment, the
Health Professions Act
, and the
Freedom
of Information and Protection of Privacy Act
…

5.         Possible
breaches of fiduciary responsibility and breaches of terms of employment …

9.         Possible
breaches of natural justice and the fundamental rights and freedoms of the
plaintiff …

10.       Possible
Charter infringements.

A.

Negligence

[
163
]

The pleadings do not disclose a reasonable basis for a cause of
action against FHA: no alleged facts to show that it owed the plaintiff duty of
care; and if so, in what regards; or the existence or nature of any loss caused
to the plaintiff. The plaintiff has not stated a factual basis to show that the
FHA may be vicariously liable for any negligent actions or omissions caused by
a hospital or a health care facility operating under FHA’s authority, as
alleged.

[
164
]

The plaintiff has not stated how the FHA’s participation in a legal
inquiry constituted a breach of a duty of care owed the FHA to the plaintiff.
She has not stated facts supporting the existence or nature of a fiduciary
obligation owed her by the FHA or why, and in what respects the FHA should be
liable for the acts or omissions of Simpson Hospital and Decker Management.
And, the plaintiff’s assertions that Simpson Hospital and/or Decker are
facilities allowed to operate under the auspices of the FHA is incorrect; and,
standing alone, form no basis for a claim that would make the FHA liable to the
plaintiff.

[
165
]

As for the plaintiff’s claim that the FHA and the HSA defamed her,
presumably through the participation of a representative of Ridge Meadows
Hospital in the investigation, thus transmitting “possibly” defamatory
statements about her; nowhere does the plaintiff recount the utterance or
writing of specific words that would tend to lower her reputation in the eyes
of a reasonable person:
Shannon v. King
,
[1931] B.C.J. No. 74
(C.A.), para. 2
. Nor does the plaintiff state the medium through which the
words alleged were communicated, when, through whom, or the nature and extent
of any damages flowing from any words allegedly defamatory. Further, to the
extent that representatives of the College questioned employees of the FHA,
they did so in their capacity as a member of the College, and absent
allegations of bad faith, such statements made in the context of an
investigation are not actionable, for much the same reasons as were discussed
in the section dealing with Decker’s application.

[
166
]

Just as with the plaintiff’s claims against the other defendants, breach
of the
FOIPPA
, various
Charter
breaches, abuse of process, bad
faith bargaining, various torts, including dignitary tort, breaches of natural
justice and so on, the findings made with respect to the other defendants apply
equally here.

[
167
]

I also agree with the FHA that, even on the most generous reading of
the further amended NCC, the plaintiff has not provided any factual or legal
basis for her claims against it: in effect, the plaintiff alleges that a Ridge
Meadows Hospital representative participated in a legal investigation, but
without any facts alleged to support a cause of action against the FHA.

[
168
]

The plaintiff’s claim must be struck under Rule 9-5 and 9-6. She has
not established a cause of action, there is no meritorious claim that deserves
to be heard, the claims are unsound in every respect required and the FHA’s answers
to it are decisive. Further, the facts pleaded do not provide a basis for any
genuine issue to be tried.

[
169
]

The plaintiff’s pleadings are struck and the FHA, together with all
the defendants is entitled to summary judgment, dismissal of all the
plaintiff’s claims against it. The claim against Ridge Meadows Hospital is also
dismissed.

IX.

Conclusion, all applications

A.

Summary Judgment

[
170
]

All the defendant applicants are entitled to the orders sought,
including summary judgment and dismissal under Rule 9-7. To this point, I have
not commented on the suitability of summary judgment and shall do that do now.

[
171
]

I was able on the whole of the evidence to find facts necessary to
decide issues of fact or law. The facts relating to the legal defences of
jurisdiction (immunity, limitation, contractual release, and the
FOIPPA
,
are straightforward and are not disputable. Furthermore, the plaintiff has not
pleaded facts that would render the defendants liable in law under the
Charter
,
in trust, or in tort, or in any other form of legal action. As stated earlier
in these reasons, the plaintiff cannot particularize an actionable claim not
for want of ability, but for want of having any facts that would form an
actionable claim.

[
172
]

I further find not only that it would not be unjust to the plaintiff
to decide the issues on summary hearing, but grossly unjust to the defendants
not to do so, considering the modest amounts involved, generously assuming the
highly unlikely event of their ever being awarded; the costs already incurred,
which have been and will be even more so in future, wholly disproportionate to
the complexity and confusing nature of the allegations; and further considering
the number of parties, to which the plaintiff intended to join others. Any
trial would be very long and drawn out, especially given the ambiguous and
poorly particularized nature of the plaintiff’s claims, and considering how
long it has taken to get to this stage, still without pleadings in actionable
or answerable form:
Inspiration Management Ltd. v. McDermid St. Lawrence
Ltd.
,
[1988] B.C.J. 1025 (C.A.)
.

[
173
]

None of the matters raised by the plaintiff in her oral submissions
address the substance of the applications. She has received and kept the
settlement funds, all matters have been addressed by the LRB and the Release
she signed, and there are no genuine claims to be tried.

[
174
]

The defendants are entitled to costs. The plaintiff’s financial
circumstances may have to be considered, but in principle, the defendants are
entitled to an order of costs. I grant leave to the parties to submit brief
written submissions, not to exceed two pages, spaced 1.5, within 21 days.

[
175
]

The interim order I made during the hearing stands and forms part of
the final order.
